blocks.html:
In Short
  • What I Did: The mode concept and pitch to the IP partner, combat balance, the UI/HUD and usability testing, plus production support for a 10-person team.
  • Hardest Problem: UEFN didn't let players pilot a mech, and the brief depended on one. I made earning the mech the match itself.
  • What it Shows: Turning a technical limit into the core hook, and keeping an external partner aligned through clear documentation.

The partner's brief asked for [a mech-centred competitive mode / players to feel the mech's scale]. At the time, UEFN only let players control their own Fortnite character, so piloting a custom vehicle such as a mech wasn't possible.

There were three obvious responses, and two were dead ends:

rows: Wait for UEFN to support it
Rejected: no date, and the partner had a schedule
Rejected: it would feel stiff and break the power fantasy
Make earning the mech the game
Chosen: the limit becomes the match's goal

blocks.html:
1. The mech is a reward, not a vehicle. Players fight to earn its power, and that fight is the match.

2. Big moments change the map. A mech strike should matter for the rest of the match, not just look good.

3. Clear in the chaos. Players always know the objective, who's winning and where the mech will strike.

Instead of working around the limit, I made it the centre of the mode. Teams fight to capture points across the map. The leading team earns the mech, a short cinematic sells its scale, and the team chooses which preset zone it strikes, reshaping that part of the map for the rest of the match.

blocks.html:
Why it Works

  • The limit drives the match. Teams must keep contesting objectives to earn the mech, so the constraint creates the action instead of slowing it.
  • Decisions that change the map. The winning team chooses where the mech strikes, changing routes and fights from then on.
  • The power fantasy survives. The activation sequence rewards the capture and shows the mech at full scale, with no piloting needed.

• Pitch and Partnership: I wrote the pitch and design documents and took them through 5+ approval rounds with the IP partner, keeping the brand's needs and the design pillars aligned. With an external partner, documentation is how a design survives: every change had to be clear enough to approve without a meeting.
  • Combat and Level Design: I owned combat balance [e.g. weapon loadouts, capture times, respawn rules] and worked with level design on pacing, engagement routes and the [N] preset strike zones.
  • Activation Cutscene: I wrote the cutscene documentation and storyboard with concept art, then coordinated animation, art and engineering so the cutscene hands back to live gameplay without breaking the match's flow.
  • UI and HUD: I designed the UI and HUD from scratch with engineering to answer three questions at a glance during heavy combat: who holds each point, how close each team is to the mech, and where it will strike.
  • Usability Tests and Production: I ran 4 usability test rounds with 10 players each, and kept the team aligned through documentation, presentations and progress reports.

• Problem: In usability tests, players couldn't tell which team was close to earning the mech. [e.g. Asked mid-match, X of Y testers couldn't say who was leading.] The mech arrived as a surprise instead of a climax.
  • Cause: Players were focused on shooting, and the score lived only in a small HUD element they never looked at. Nothing in the world signalled that the mech was getting close.

Options Considered:
  • Bigger score numbers. Rejected: still easy to miss mid-fight, and it cluttered the screen.
  • Frequent announcer callouts. Rejected: it would become noise over a long match.
  • Redesign the score display around Fortnite's own HUD conventions, with cues that escalate near the threshold. Chosen.

Fix: I rebuilt the score UI to match the layout Fortnite players already know, with Gundam-styled shapes and colours. The display grows more prominent as a team nears the mech, and a world-space marker on the strike zone.

Result: Players began changing strategy as the score neared the threshold, either pushing to close it out or swarming the leader's points to deny them. In the next tests, 7 of 10 testers could name the leading team.

• Earned mech over fake piloting. Players never steer the mech, which some fans may expect, but the mode gained a clear goal and kept its power fantasy.
  • Preset strike zones over free targeting. Free targeting would have given players more control, but every possible strike would have needed to look good, stay balanced and run within UEFN's limits. [N] hand-built zones meant each strike reliably opened new routes, and level design could test every outcome.
  • Scope call, a short cutscene ~50s so the match never stalls.

What Worked: Turning the engine limit into the match's goal.

What I'd do Differently: Prototype the strike zones before writing the cutscene. Building the cutscene first meant re-aligning concept art, animation and level design when the zones changed, which cost almost 2 weeks.

What I Learned: An engine limit can become the best idea in the design if you ask what it makes players do. With an external partner, clear documentation is the design.
